:::{#thm-density-not-unique}
#### A density is not unique

If $f$ is a [density](#def-pdf) of a continuous random variable $X$,
and $g \ge 0$ differs from $f$ at only finitely many points,
then $g$ is also a density of $X$.

:::

::: proof

For $a \le b$,
the difference $g - f$ is $0$ at all but finitely many points, so:

$$
\ba
\int_a^b g(x)\,dx
&= \int_a^b f(x)\,dx + \int_a^b \paren{g(x) - f(x)}\,dx
&& \text{(linearity of the integral)} \\
&= \int_a^b f(x)\,dx + 0
&& \text{(a function that is 0 at all but finitely many points integrates to 0)} \\
&= \Pr(a \le X \le b)
&& \text{(} f \text{ is a density of } X \text{)}
\ea
$$

Together with $g \ge 0$, this is @def-pdf for $g$.

:::
